question: In the individual participant data meta-analysis of vitamin D supplementation, what effect did supplementation have on acute respiratory tract infection, and how did that effect differ by dosing schedule and baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D status?
options: It reduced infection risk overall, with the clearest benefit in participants given daily or weekly doses without boluses and in those with very low baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
It reduced infection risk only when given as one or more bolus doses.
It had no effect on infection risk in any subgroup.
It increased infection risk among participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol/L.
gold_answer: It reduced infection risk overall, with the clearest benefit in participants given daily or weekly doses without boluses and in those with very low baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
notes: Calibration item. Every passage was checked against PMC5310969 on 2026-11-19. Human verification, independent annotation, and adjudication are required. Option D is an unused distractor; agents 0 and 2 argue different incorrect positions so the item tests evidence-weighted trust rather than simple vote counting.

positions.answer: It reduced infection risk only when given as one or more bolus doses.

claims.text: Supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection only among participants receiving one or more bolus doses.

evidence.text: In subgroup analysis, protective effects were seen in those receiving daily or weekly vitamin D without additional bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.81, 0.72 to 0.91) but not in those receiving one or more bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 0.86 to 1.10; P for interaction=0.05).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage reports protective effects in participants receiving daily or weekly vitamin D without bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.81) and no protective effect in those receiving bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 0.86 to 1.10), the reverse of the claim.

claims.text: The meta-analysis identified 25 eligible randomised controlled trials.

evidence.text: 25 eligible randomised controlled trials (total 11 321 participants, aged 0 to 95 years) were identified.
evidence.notes: Excerpted clause from the Results sentence describing study selection.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that 25 eligible randomised controlled trials were identified, which directly entails the claim.

claims.text: The observed reduction in infection risk was confined to participants who took supplements during winter months.

evidence.text: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection among all participants (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.81 to 0.96; P for heterogeneity <0.001).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives the overall effect and its confidence interval but contains no seasonal or winter-month comparison, so it neither establishes nor refutes a restriction to winter supplementation.

positions.answer: It reduced infection risk overall, with the clearest benefit in participants given daily or weekly doses without boluses and in those with very low baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

claims.text: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection among all participants, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.88.

evidence.text: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection among all participants (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.81 to 0.96; P for heterogeneity <0.001).

claims.text: Protective effects were seen in participants receiving daily or weekly vitamin D without additional bolus doses, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.81.

evidence.text: In subgroup analysis, protective effects were seen in those receiving daily or weekly vitamin D without additional bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.81, 0.72 to 0.91) but not in those receiving one or more bolus doses (adjusted odds ratio 0.97, 0.86 to 1.10; P for interaction=0.05).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage explicitly reports protective effects for daily or weekly vitamin D without additional bolus doses, adjusted odds ratio 0.81 (0.72 to 0.91).

claims.text: Among participants receiving daily or weekly vitamin D, protection was stronger when baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D was below 25 nmol/L than when it was at least 25 nmol/L.

evidence.text: Among those receiving daily or weekly vitamin D, protective effects were stronger in those with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels <25 nmol/L (adjusted odds ratio 0.30, 0.17 to 0.53) than in those with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels ≥25 nmol/L (adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 0.60 to 0.95; P for interaction=0.006).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage directly compares the two baseline groups, reporting adjusted odds ratios of 0.30 below 25 nmol/L and 0.75 at or above 25 nmol/L, with P for interaction 0.006.

positions.answer: It had no effect on infection risk in any subgroup.

claims.text: Supplementation had no effect on the risk of acute respiratory tract infection among all participants.

evidence.text: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection among all participants (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.81 to 0.96; P for heterogeneity <0.001).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage reports a reduced risk among all participants (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.96), which refutes the claim of no overall effect.

claims.text: Vitamin D supplementation did not influence the proportion of participants experiencing at least one serious adverse event.

evidence.text: Vitamin D did not influence the proportion of participants experiencing at least one serious adverse event (adjusted odds ratio 0.98, 0.80 to 1.20, P=0.83).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that vitamin D did not influence the proportion of participants with at least one serious adverse event (adjusted odds ratio 0.98, P=0.83), which entails the claim.

claims.text: The effect of supplementation on infection risk was independent of baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration.

evidence.text: Among those receiving daily or weekly vitamin D, protective effects were stronger in those with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels <25 nmol/L (adjusted odds ratio 0.30, 0.17 to 0.53) than in those with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels ≥25 nmol/L (adjusted odds ratio 0.75, 0.60 to 0.95; P for interaction=0.006).

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage reports stronger protective effects below 25 nmol/L than at or above it, with P for interaction 0.006, so the effect was not independent of baseline status.
